title: The Flipside of Potential
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles contends that hard-working, well-qualified teachers fall short because of school leadership, not their own failings. He notes that teachers work unpaid hours and are left alone in classrooms without much help improving. He lists five leadership problems: not knowing efficient ways to raise progress, missing the curriculum as the best teacher training, observing behaviours instead of the curriculum, using assessment to rank rather than to teach, and fractured leadership. He ends with advice to teachers to recognise the cause and become the leader who fixes these things in their own class or team. The piece is instructional-leadership commentary with a strong curriculum-first stance.
points: Teacher effort is abundant, but isolation and weak training mean some crops flourish and others do not.
The curriculum is presented as the fastest route to training every teacher, so CPD should centre on it.
Lesson visits should examine the curriculum and what students do, not low-impact teacher behaviours like questioning.
Assessment should serve retrieval, curriculum adjustment and experiments rather than ranking students.
Leaders and middle leaders should work as one team on the curriculum rather than defending individual roles.
quotes: Imagine a driving instructor letting you loose in a car, giving you occasional instructions from your radio. You’d just be thrilled to get from A to B without smashing anything. That’s a teacher’s daily life.

Teachers are like land owners preparing a fantastically rich soil. It’s fertile, overflowing with potential. But they know little about farming, and so some crops flourish, and others don’t, even though they are out in the fields every single day.
A teacher will naturally ask themselves this horrible question. If we, our school and our students, have so much potential, I must be really terrible at my job to mess it up. Am I the problem?

Leaders don’t realise the curriculum is the quickest and best way to train all their teachers. A thoughtful curriculum will train every teacher in what students need to know, how they will learn it and how they will retain it in long term memory.

Lesson visits focus on teacher behaviour rather than improving the curriculum: what students do. So leaders try to improve low impact things like ‘questioning’, instead of making students work and think hard about what teachers value most: the curriculum.
Fractured leadership is the norm in SLT meetings, meetings of middle leaders, and department meetings. Or worse, the meeting is simply information giving.
